text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's Austrian newspapers.
DER STANDARD

- Social Democrat Chancellor Franz Vranitzky wants to serve to the end of his term, he said in an interview after his party suffered its worst vote in democratic Austria. He said he would remain party leader until 1999, when the next federal elections should take place. A change in the government is not planned either.
- Transport and Science Minister Rudolf Scholten is planning to use about three billion schillings from the ERP on subsidies for hi-tech firms over the next three years.
- Groceries are not willing to accept a reduction in opening hours to 60 hours a week from 66 hours to allow for longer shopping hours on Saturdays.
- Grocer Billa will keep up its ecologically friendly Ja!-Natuerlich line under its new owner German Rewe. The turnover in this area should double from its current one billion schillngs by 1999.
- Steel maker Boehler-Uddeholm is going to raise its capacity for high-quality steel to 36,500 tonnes a year from 27,000 through investments worth 200 million schillings.
DIE PRESSE

- Austria's government coalition is divided over reforming state benefits, having praised reforms as the only way forward after Sunday's European parliamentary election results, in which the far right Freedom Party made huge gains.
- Austria's financial standing has moved down a place in Euromoney's listing and is now rated in ninth position.
- 270 workers have been given notice by steelmaker Boehler Edelstahl in an early warning system for job losses.
- Trade Minister Hannes Farnleitner wants to get more small intensive research businesses into Austria, as he believes the time of major investors has passed.
- Cigarette maker Reemtsma wants to take over Austria Tabak. However the government will only put it to tender next year.
KURIER
- Far-right Freedom Party leader Joerg Haider sees himself as the new working class leader and the political heir of Austria's former socialist Chancellor Bruno Kreisky.
- For the first time in ten years the price of diesel is over ten schillings.
WIRTSCHAFTSBLATT
- A U.S. study shows that Austrian bureaucracy is slowing down economic growth in the country.
- Grocery chain Meinl is planning to open 30 shops by the end of 1997.
- The consortium around EA-Generali is pinning its hopes on Die Erste savings bank coming back into the consortium.
SALZBURGER NACHRICHTEN

- Austrian investors Hammerer and Turnauer or Liaunig and Bank Austria look likely candidates for the takeover of aluminium maker Amag. German aluminium maker VAW is not seen with a chance in the bidding due to the ongoing debate in Austria over selling off firms to foreign investors.
